slides.text: Welcome to Module 5, Reasoning with SQL Logic. Earlier modules focused on retrieving rows, changing data safely, and creating summaries. Now we focus on the rules that decide which rows qualify and how values should be classified. Real data is not always simple: conditions overlap, fields may be missing, and SQL can produce an UNKNOWN truth state. We will work with AND, OR, and NOT, then study TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN. We will use NULL-safe tools such as IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, COALESCE, and NULLIF, and we will build CASE expressions where branch order matters. The main habit is to reason before writing syntax: state the rule, decide how missing values should behave, write the SQL, and test edge cases.

Module 4 asked questions such as how many, how much, or what is the average. Module 5 asks a different question: which rule applies? A decision rule can involve several conditions at once. For example, a record might qualify only when it is active, consent is explicitly true, a diagnosis belongs to a target set, and usable contact information is missing. Some of those fields may be NULL. That is why this module emphasizes structure. Define the condition, inspect missingness, group related tests with parentheses, order CASE branches carefully, and test boundary values such as zero, blank text, FALSE, and NULL. The goal is not merely SQL that runs. The goal is SQL whose output matches the written rule.

By the end of this module, you should be able to compose Boolean conditions, explain SQL's three-valued logic, and handle missing values deliberately. You will learn when to use IS NULL, IS TRUE, IS FALSE, IS UNKNOWN, and IS DISTINCT FROM. You will use COALESCE for fallback logic and NULLIF for normalization and safe ratios. You will build searched and simple CASE expressions with clear boundaries and explicit handling of missing values. Finally, you will combine these tools in realistic rules and explain why each row was included, excluded, or classified. These are reasoning skills rather than memorization tasks. If you understand why the query behaves as it does, adapting it to a new dataset becomes much easier.

This six-step workflow is the foundation for the module. First, state the rule in plain language. Second, identify which fields can be missing. Third, group related Boolean tests with parentheses, especially when AND and OR appear together. Fourth, when using CASE, put specific or high-priority branches before broad branches because the first true branch wins. Fifth, test edge cases such as exact thresholds, zero, empty text, whitespace, FALSE, and NULL. Finally, compare the output with the written rule. This workflow prevents a common kind of SQL problem: a statement that is syntactically correct and runs without an error, but quietly returns the wrong cohort or label.

The practice database contains four small tables and one convenience view. patient_info includes demographics, contacts, activity status, consent, and preferred language. diagnostics adds diagnosis, severity, and confirmation state. patient_billing includes bill amounts, payments, and payment status. admissions contains admission and discharge dates. The patient_case view combines the first three tables so this module can focus on logic rather than join syntax. The data intentionally includes NULL values, empty strings, whitespace-only strings, a zero bill, a missing payment status, and an unknown consent value. Those edge cases make the logic visible. Everything is synthetic and disposable, so students can experiment safely.

AND, OR, and NOT are the basic building blocks of SQL decision rules. AND requires all connected conditions to be true. OR requires at least one. NOT reverses a known Boolean result. SQL also has UNKNOWN, usually because a comparison involves NULL. That extra state changes how some compound expressions behave. Think about the practical effect: AND usually narrows a cohort, OR usually broadens it, and NOT excludes a condition only when the truth state is known. The next slides separate the operators so you can see their behavior before combining them with missing values and precedence rules.

AND means every connected condition must be true for the row to qualify. Here the record must be active, the age must be at least forty, and severity must be High. If any one condition is false, the row does not remain. Run the query and inspect the result. Then imagine removing one condition and notice that the cohort would usually become larger. A useful beginner habit is to read the WHERE clause as a sentence. If the sentence requires several things at the same time, AND is usually the correct connector. If you intended alternatives, OR may be more appropriate.

OR represents alternatives. A row remains when at least one condition is true. In this example, the diagnosis can be Pneumonia, Flu, or Asthma. This normally broadens the result because several different values can qualify. When multiple OR conditions compare the same column with a list of values, IN can often express the rule more compactly. The important idea is that OR does not require all options to be true. Any qualifying alternative is enough. Later, when OR is mixed with AND, parentheses become especially important because the grouping of those conditions changes the meaning.

NOT negates a Boolean expression. In this example, active records are kept while selected diagnoses are excluded. Parentheses make the target of NOT clear: the entire IN expression is being negated. With ordinary true and false values, NOT reverses the result. But SQL also has UNKNOWN. If an expression is unknown because it depends on NULL, NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN. That matters because WHERE keeps only true rows. Use NOT when the exclusion rule is clear, but be careful when nullable values are involved. Sometimes an explicit NULL-safe predicate communicates the rule more accurately.

PostgreSQL has a precedence order for logical operators. NOT is evaluated before AND, and AND is evaluated before OR. So A OR B AND C means A OR the combination of B AND C. Knowing that rule is useful, but relying on memory is risky. Parentheses make the intended business logic visible and protect the rule when another person edits the query later. For this course, treat parentheses as documentation. When AND and OR appear together, group the related tests explicitly so the query is easier to explain and harder to misread.

These two conditions look similar, but they represent different policies. Without parentheses, AND is evaluated first, so the consent requirement applies only to the Kidney Disease branch. Any patient age sixty-five or older can qualify even when consent is false. With parentheses, the age and diagnosis alternatives are grouped together, and explicit consent is required for the entire rule. Run both statements and compare the rows. Lisa Ray is the useful boundary record: age seventy-one, but consent is false. She appears only in the unparenthesized version. This is why parentheses are part of the meaning, not just formatting.

SQL does not use only two truth states. When NULL is involved, a condition can become UNKNOWN. NULL means missing, unknown, or not applicable. It is not zero, an empty string, a space, or false. Because SQL does not know the missing value, ordinary comparisons involving NULL often cannot be proven true or false. The result is UNKNOWN. The practical rule to remember is that WHERE keeps only TRUE. FALSE rows are excluded, and UNKNOWN rows are also excluded. A row can disappear not because a condition was definitely false, but because the data was insufficient to prove it true.

Three-valued logic becomes easier when you inspect a few important combinations. TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN because the unknown side could still be false. FALSE AND UNKNOWN is definitely false because one false value is enough. TRUE OR UNKNOWN is definitely true because one true value is enough. FALSE OR UNKNOWN remains unknown because the unknown side could still be true. NOT UNKNOWN remains unknown. Run the truth table and scan the combinations. You do not need to memorize every row. Instead, ask whether the known part of the expression is already enough to determine the final result.

This slide isolates one rule that explains many NULL-related surprises: WHERE keeps only TRUE. The example creates three rows with Boolean states true, false, and NULL, then applies WHERE flag. Only the true row remains. The false row is removed as expected, and the unknown row is also removed because SQL cannot prove the condition true. This matters when a nullable field such as consent is used in a filter. Decide whether unknown values should be excluded, included for review, or treated separately. Do not let WHERE's default behavior make that policy decision accidentally.

A common beginner mistake is writing equals NULL. That does not test whether a value is missing. It asks whether a known value is equal to an unknown value, and SQL cannot prove the comparison. The result is UNKNOWN, even for rows where the column is NULL. The same issue affects not-equal NULL. SQL provides explicit missing-value predicates: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. Run the example and inspect the calculated columns. You should see NULL results instead of useful true or false answers. When the question is whether a value is missing, use IS NULL. Treat that as a basic SQL habit.

A blank string is not NULL in PostgreSQL. An empty string is a known text value with zero characters, and a whitespace-only string is also a real value until spaces are removed. This matters when a rule says no usable email. Testing only IS NULL would miss empty text and whitespace-only text. BTRIM removes surrounding spaces. NULLIF then converts an empty trimmed result to NULL. After that normalization, IS NULL can treat the three cases consistently. Run the example and inspect the patients returned. This is a practical preparation pattern because messy text often needs normalization before business rules are applied.

A nullable Boolean can represent three different states. Consent can be explicitly true, explicitly false, or unknown because no value was recorded. Those states may have very different meanings. Explicit false can mean do not contact. Unknown may mean send the record for review rather than treating it as a refusal. PostgreSQL provides IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN. Run the example and inspect the patient whose consent is NULL. explicitly_yes and explicitly_no should both be false, while not_recorded is true. This pattern is useful whenever a Boolean field represents permission, approval, or verification and unknown is not equivalent to no.

IS DISTINCT FROM is useful when you need a definite comparison between nullable values. Ordinary equality or inequality can become UNKNOWN when NULL is involved. IS DISTINCT FROM avoids that uncertainty. Two equal non-NULL values are not distinct. Two NULL values are also treated as not distinct. A NULL compared with a non-NULL value is distinct. The companion predicate IS NOT DISTINCT FROM works like NULL-safe equality. Run the example and focus on rows containing NULL. The output still contains true or false rather than unknown. Use these predicates when missingness is part of the comparison itself.

COALESCE evaluates expressions from left to right and returns the first one that is not NULL. That makes it useful for fallback logic. A preferred contact rule might try email first, then mobile phone, then home phone, and finally a readable message. But COALESCE only understands NULL. An empty string or whitespace-only string is still non-NULL and can stop the fallback too early. That is why COALESCE is often combined with NULLIF and trimming. Be careful with numeric defaults as well. Replacing a missing bill with zero makes a strong domain assumption. Use a fallback only when its meaning is intentional and documented.

NULLIF compares two expressions. When they are equal, it returns NULL; otherwise it returns the first expression. A useful text-cleaning pattern is NULLIF of trimmed text and an empty string. BTRIM removes surrounding whitespace, and NULLIF converts the empty result to NULL. This gives several representations of no usable text one consistent missing-value state. Run the query and compare original_email with normalized_email. Normal email values remain unchanged, while empty or whitespace-only text becomes NULL. This small transformation makes later IS NULL and COALESCE logic easier to reason about.

This example combines normalization and fallback logic. We want the first usable contact method, but an empty email or a string containing only spaces should not block the fallback. Each contact value is trimmed, and NULLIF converts an empty result to NULL. COALESCE then chooses the first available value. The order expresses priority: email, then mobile, then home, then a final label. Run the query and inspect the edge cases. Robert Lee and Lisa Ray should fall back to home phone. Maria Torres should use mobile because her email contains only spaces. Andre Green should receive the final No contact provided label.

NULLIF is also useful for numeric safety. Division by zero is an error, and the practice data includes a zero bill. NULLIF bill_amount, zero converts an exact zero denominator to NULL. Division by NULL then returns NULL rather than raising an error. Here that means the percentage is not computable, which is different from zero percent. The numerator uses COALESCE amount_paid to zero, which is a separate assumption that should be justified by the domain. Run the query and inspect the No Charge record. Safe SQL should avoid errors while preserving the meaning of the data.

CASE creates derived values without modifying the stored table. PostgreSQL checks WHEN clauses from top to bottom. As soon as one WHEN condition is true, CASE stops and returns that branch's THEN expression. Later branches are not evaluated for that row. If no WHEN matches, ELSE is used; if ELSE is omitted, the result is NULL. This makes branch order part of the rule. A broad branch placed too early can make a more specific branch unreachable. Before writing CASE, identify overlapping conditions and decide which outcomes have higher priority. Specific exceptions and higher thresholds usually belong before broader defaults.

Searched CASE is the flexible form of CASE. Each WHEN contains a complete Boolean condition, so it works well for ranges, compound rules, and NULL checks. The billing example handles NULL first so a missing amount is not silently classified as low. It then checks the highest threshold, followed by the next threshold, and uses ELSE for the remaining known values. A twelve-thousand-dollar bill matches High-Value and stops there. A seventy-five-hundred-dollar bill reaches Standard. Run the example and inspect zero, NULL, and threshold values. Searched CASE is especially useful when the business rule itself needs to be visible in the SQL.

Simple CASE compares one expression with a list of exact values. It is a good fit for direct code-to-label mappings. In this example, Paid and No Charge map to Closed, Open maps to Follow up, Pending Review maps to Investigate, and anything else reaches ELSE. The row with a NULL payment status therefore becomes Status missing. Simple CASE is concise when the rule is based on exact values. It is not the best form for ranges such as amount greater than or equal to five thousand; searched CASE is clearer for that. Run the query and compare the mapped actions.

Branch order matters when CASE conditions overlap. If age greater than or equal to eighteen comes first, every senior also satisfies that condition, so the senior branch can never run. The correct order places the more specific senior threshold first, then the broader adult threshold. Run both versions and inspect the classifications for the older patients. This is the same general rule you will use for billing tiers and priority labels: place specific or high-priority conditions before broad conditions. If one branch logically contains another, the narrower branch normally needs to come first.

A good tiering rule makes its boundaries explicit. In the source rule, NULL is handled first as Unknown. Amounts of ten thousand or more are High-Value. Amounts of five thousand or more, but below ten thousand, are Standard. Remaining known amounts are Low-Value. Because the thresholds are written from high to low, each amount reaches the intended branch. An exact ten thousand belongs to High-Value, and an exact five thousand belongs to Standard. Later practice adds a separate No Charge category for an exact zero. When you design tiers, test NULL, zero, exact thresholds, and values just above and below each boundary.

If a CASE expression has no ELSE and no WHEN branch matches, PostgreSQL returns NULL. That can be intentional when NULL means unclassified, but it can also create ambiguity if the analyst expected a value such as Other. The example labels respiratory diagnoses and leaves all other diagnoses NULL. Run it and inspect the unmatched rows. Before omitting ELSE, decide what the missing result means. The same idea applies when the input can be NULL. If a missing measure needs a separate category such as Needs review, add an explicit NULL branch rather than letting the value fall through accidentally.

The most dangerous logic errors are often not syntax errors. PostgreSQL executes the statement successfully, but the result does not match the intended rule. Mixed AND and OR can be grouped incorrectly. Equals NULL cannot test missingness. NOT IN can behave unexpectedly when the list contains NULL. Ordinary not-equal excludes a missing value as UNKNOWN. CASE can hide a specific rule behind a broader earlier branch. Because these statements run without a syntax error, prediction and edge-case testing are essential. Whenever logic matters, test records with NULL, zero, blank text, FALSE, exact thresholds, and values that satisfy more than one condition.

NOT IN can be surprising when the list contains NULL. Conceptually, the predicate asks whether a value is different from every item in the list. If one item is unknown, PostgreSQL cannot prove that an ordinary value is different from that unknown value. The result can become UNKNOWN instead of true. Because WHERE keeps only true, rows that look like obvious non-matches may disappear. Run the example and inspect the output. The safer pattern is to keep NULL out of the list and handle missing status explicitly with IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, or another NULL-safe predicate. Make the missing-value policy visible in the query.

This comparison makes NULL policy very concrete. With ordinary not-equal, a NULL payment status does not produce true. It produces UNKNOWN, so the row is removed by WHERE. IS DISTINCT FROM returns a definite answer. A NULL status is distinct from the text Paid, so that row is included. Neither rule is universally correct. The right choice depends on the question. If you want only known statuses that are not Paid, ordinary inequality may match the rule. If you want everything that is not definitely Paid, including missing status for review, IS DISTINCT FROM is better. Run both statements and compare the row counts.

This applied query combines several ideas from the module into one cohort rule. The record must be active. Consent must be explicitly true, which means NULL consent is not treated as permission. The diagnosis must be either Diabetes or Kidney Disease. Finally, the email field is normalized so NULL, empty text, and whitespace-only text all count as unavailable. Every condition is connected with AND because all requirements must be satisfied. Run the query and inspect the result. Robert Lee is a useful record because the diagnosis is Kidney Disease, consent is true, and email is NULL. Susan Gray has Kidney Disease but consent is unknown, so the row should not qualify.

This report combines contact normalization and CASE classification in one output. For contact information, blank and whitespace-only text are normalized before COALESCE selects the first usable contact method. For billing, the query makes a different decision. A missing bill is not converted to zero. Instead, CASE labels it Needs review. An exact zero gets No Charge, then higher tiers are checked from specific thresholds down to the low-value default. Sometimes a fallback is appropriate for display. Other times a missing value carries data-quality meaning that should remain visible. Run the query and compare the NULL bill record with the zero bill record.

This example shows how population filtering and CASE classification work together. The rule concerns completed stays, so the WHERE clause first removes admissions with no discharge date. That prevents an ongoing stay from being forced into a category that requires a completed duration. PostgreSQL can subtract one date from another and return the number of days. CASE then classifies the duration as Short for fewer than five days, Medium for five through ten days, and Long for anything greater than ten. Run the query and inspect the boundary values. A five-day stay should be Medium. The broader lesson is to define the population before applying a classification rule.

Time-based rules can change from day to day if they use the current system date. For teaching and grading, that can make results hard to reproduce. The source module therefore uses a fixed reference date: August 11, 2026. The WHERE clause selects admissions from the preceding thirty days and keeps Pneumonia or Flu diagnoses. The CASE expression identifies high-risk respiratory cases when the patient is at least sixty years old. Other respiratory cases receive a simpler label. Run the query and inspect the dates. Because the reference date is fixed, every student should get the same result even when they run the lesson later.

The reasoning patterns in this module transfer well across SQL systems, but exact syntax can differ. AND, OR, NOT, IS NULL, COALESCE, NULLIF, and CASE are broadly familiar across databases. IS DISTINCT FROM is supported in PostgreSQL and some modern systems, but you should check the target platform. Date arithmetic is especially variable. PostgreSQL can subtract dates directly, while SQL Server and Microsoft Fabric commonly use functions such as DATEDIFF. The best transfer strategy is to preserve the rule first. Define the cohort, decide how NULL should behave, group mixed conditions with parentheses, order CASE branches, and test boundary records. Translate dialect-specific functions after the logic is correct.

For this guided practice, predict before you run. Compare the unparenthesized rule with the parenthesized rule. Because AND binds before OR, Version A allows any patient age sixty-five or older even when consent is not true. Version B applies the consent requirement to both alternatives. Look for the record that satisfies the age condition but has false consent. That record should appear only in Version A. The purpose is not just to identify the row. Explain which subexpression admitted it. If you can say that the age branch was evaluated independently of consent because AND bound to the diagnosis branch, you understand the precedence problem.

This guided practice applies the normalization pattern to a different column. The stored table should not be changed. We only want a display value in the query result. Start by trimming preferred_language. Use NULLIF to convert an empty trimmed value to NULL. Then use COALESCE to replace the missing result with Language not recorded. The practice data includes one patient whose preferred language is NULL. Run the query and confirm that the stored column remains NULL while the derived language_display column shows the fallback label. A SELECT expression can standardize output without overwriting source data.

This practice refines the billing CASE by giving an exact zero bill its own category. The order is deliberate. Check NULL first so missing values are not confused with zero. Then check bill_amount equals zero and label it No Charge. After that, test the high and standard thresholds, and use ELSE for the remaining positive low-value bills. Run the query and inspect patient 107, whose bill is exactly zero. That record should now show No Charge rather than Low-Value. This demonstrates how domain meaning affects branch design.

This guided practice is about policy, not just syntax. Run the two status filters from the earlier slide and compare the results. Ordinary not-equal excludes the NULL status because the comparison becomes UNKNOWN. IS DISTINCT FROM returns true for NULL compared with Paid, so the missing-status record is included. The additional row is Susan Gray's billing record, where payment_status is NULL. Now explain the business meaning. The first query means known status and not Paid. The second query means anything that is not definitely Paid, including a missing status that may need review. Both can be valid. The important skill is choosing the one that matches the intended rule.

This practice changes only the reference date in the recent respiratory report. Replace August 11, 2026 with August 5, 2026 and think about the new thirty-day window. Before running, identify which admissions are near the boundaries. Moving the reference date earlier changes which dates qualify, but it does not change patient ages or the age-sixty risk threshold. This separation is important. The WHERE clause defines the cohort. The CASE expression classifies the rows that remain. A change to the population does not automatically change the classification rule. After predicting, run the revised query and compare the set of admissions with the original result.

Coding Exercise 1 checks whether you can translate a mixed AND and OR rule correctly. The two alternatives are age sixty-five or older and Kidney Disease. Those belong together inside parentheses. Then explicit consent must apply to the entire grouped condition. Your result should include only the columns requested in the starter. Before clicking Run and Check, read the WHERE clause aloud. It should sound like age sixty-five or older, or Kidney Disease, and in either case consent must be explicitly true. If a patient with false consent appears, review the placement of the parentheses. This exercise is designed to catch exactly the precedence error we studied earlier.

Coding Exercise 2 combines text normalization and fallback logic. Do not use COALESCE directly on the raw email field because an empty string or whitespace-only string is not NULL. Normalize each contact field first with BTRIM and NULLIF. Then use COALESCE in the requested priority order: email, mobile phone, home phone, and finally No contact provided. After running, inspect the edge cases. Robert Lee should fall back to home phone. Lisa Ray should also use home phone. Maria Torres should use mobile because the email contains only spaces. Andre Green should receive the final fallback text.

Coding Exercise 3 asks you to build a searched CASE with clear boundaries. Begin with an explicit NULL branch. Then add exact zero as No Charge. Next add the high-value threshold and the standard threshold, in that order. Use ELSE for the remaining known positive bills. The order matters because CASE stops at the first true branch. The NULL branch preserves missingness as Unknown rather than classifying it as low. The zero branch separates a no-charge state from a low-value charge. After running, inspect patient 103, patient 107, patient 101, and patient 102. Those records exercise the main branches of the rule.

Coding Exercise 4 tests whether you can encode a policy that includes missing status. The wording is not definitely Paid. That means a NULL status should remain in the result for review. Ordinary not-equal does not satisfy that policy because NULL compared with Paid becomes UNKNOWN and is filtered out. Use IS DISTINCT FROM to get a definite Boolean result. After running, you should see six billing rows. The missing status record is an important part of the expected result. This short exercise captures an important distinction between a known non-Paid status and a status that is simply not known to be Paid.

Coding Exercise 5 combines a population filter, a derived measure, and CASE classification. First, keep only completed admissions using discharge_date IS NOT NULL. Then calculate length_of_stay_days by subtracting admission_date from discharge_date. Build the categories exactly as defined: Short for fewer than five days, Medium for five through ten days, and Long for more than ten days. Check the boundary behavior carefully. A five-day stay belongs in Medium, not Short. A twelve-day stay belongs in Long. The expected result contains six completed admissions. If ongoing admissions appear, review the WHERE clause before changing the CASE expression.

Coding Exercise 6 brings the entire module together in one CASE expression. The highest-priority rule is Do not contact for inactive records or explicit refusal. Put that first. Next comes the specific Urgent rule: active, explicit consent, high severity, and no usable email. Then the broader Routine rule covers active patients with explicit consent who did not match Urgent. Everything else becomes Review. Branch order matters. If Routine comes before Urgent, the urgent branch becomes unreachable for consenting active patients. The exercise also requires NULL-aware email handling. Blank and whitespace-only email should count as unavailable.

This is the final completion step for Assignment 5. The slide deck tracks ten knowledge checks and six coding exercises, for sixteen required activities in total. Before selecting Complete Module, review the counters. If anything is missing, the page will list incomplete activities and let you jump back to the relevant slide. When you complete the module, the page creates a Canvas submission summary that includes your knowledge-check status and the SQL from each coding exercise. Review the report before copying it. Your work is stored locally in the current browser, so it may not follow you to another device, private window, or cleared browser storage.

Let us close Module 5 by connecting the main ideas. AND, OR, and NOT build compound rules, but mixed conditions should be grouped with parentheses so the intended logic is visible. SQL uses TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE. NULL is not the same as zero or blank text. Use IS NULL for missingness, Boolean predicates for nullable true and false fields, and IS DISTINCT FROM when you need a definite comparison involving NULL. NULLIF can normalize sentinel values such as blank text or zero denominators. COALESCE can choose the first available fallback when the fallback reflects a documented rule. CASE evaluates from top to bottom, so specific overlapping branches belong before broad ones. Finally, validate edge cases.
